action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab is primary instrument for period measurement. Before examining other instruments or making predictions, I need a second day of measurements on the same apparatus under identical conditions to detect any systematic drift, temperature effects, or instrumental creep. This is foundational: without a baseline drift characterization, I cannot interpret anomalies or validate the precision measurement programme. Post-baseline data will also allow me to compute confidence in future single-trial readings and establish whether this instrument is stable enough for publication-grade work.

The 24 existing readings show no anomalies (24 distinct values, no exact repetitions, no level shifts), consistent with random instrumental noise. Continuing baseline data collection is the only action that advances the core goal: establishing a reliable baseline against which future drift or shifts can be detected.

Day 11 continuation of baseline monitoring. The day 10 excursion cluster (trials 85–87, 89) demands immediate replication under controlled conditions. Running trials 95–106 today will test whether: (1) elevated periods persist (supporting temperature drift hypothesis if lab remains warm, or instrument drift if monotonic increase continues), (2) values return to baseline mean ~1.6681 (supporting day 10 procedural variance or transient environmental disturbance), or (3) scatter pattern repeats (supporting systematic rather than random cause). Temperature sensor cross-check will be recorded simultaneously. This is the highest-priority disambiguator before any other instrument cross-checks, because if pendulum_lab itself is drifting or temperature-sensitive, all downstream interpretations are compromised. Day 11's 10 trials (97–106) show mean 1.6759, only z=1.53 above baseline—a modest drift that does not yet confirm the day 10 excursion pattern. Temperature drift (p=0.42) and calibration drift (p=0.28) remain the leading hypotheses, both predicting continued monotonic or scattered elevation. Running 12 fresh trials today will (1) test whether day 10's cluster (trials 85–87, 89) was transient or part of a persistent trend, (2) accumulate power to detect true drift vs. noise, and (3) allow real-time temperature logging (currently absent from my records—a critical gap). If today's trials cluster high again, temperature or calibration drift is strengthened; if they revert toward 1.6681, procedural variance or transient environmental disturbance on day 10 becomes favored. This is the highest-leverage test to disambiguate between my top two hypotheses and move toward replication-quality claims. I must also log ambient temperature during these trials to begin validating the temperature hypothesis directly.

Cross-instrument validation is critical. Day 10 excursions in pendulum_lab cluster at high values, but I have NOT yet measured pendulum_obs systematically since baseline. If the day 10 anomaly is environmental (temperature, gravity, or procedural), pendulum_obs should show a similar pattern. If pendulum_obs remains stable on day 13, that argues AGAINST settlement-wide physical changes and FOR instrument-local or lab-local drift (temperature in lab enclosure, calibration drift in pendulum_lab's timing mechanism, or day-10-specific procedural variance). If pendulum_obs ALSO shows elevated values, that points toward genuine geophysical change or settlement-wide thermal shift. Either way, the independent measurement will disambiguate competing hypotheses at p=0.42 (temperature) vs p=0.28 (instrument drift) vs p=0.08 (physical). This is the highest-value replication check I can execute today and aligns with my core principle: no claim without independent validation.

state.question: Why do trials 85–87 and 89 show elevated period values (≥1.6755 beats), breaking the baseline stability observed in trials 1–84?

hypotheses.label: Temperature drift in pendulum lab (ambient or apparatus)
hypotheses.rationale: Elevated periods in days 9–10 (trials 73–94) cluster toward higher values, with marked excursions on day 10 (trials 85, 86, 87, 89). A slow warming trend would increase the pendulum's length or change material properties, lengthening period. This is the most parsimonious explanation for a monotonic upward drift. Day 10 excursions could reflect lab heating. Temperature is easily reproducible and measurable—critical for baseline validation.

hypotheses.label: Instrument calibration drift (timing mechanism slowing)
hypotheses.rationale: If the timing mechanism (clock, oscillator) has drifted fractionally slow over days 1–10, *all* measured periods would be artificially lengthened relative to true physical period. This would manifest as upward drift in the recorded series and would not reset between trials. Day 10 excursions are consistent with cumulative drift. However, this predicts monotonic increase, not the scatter observed; scattered high values on day 10 argue against pure drift.

hypotheses.label: Measurement procedure variance on day 10 (operator fatigue, technique shift, or environmental disturbance)
hypotheses.rationale: Scattered high values on day 10 (trials 85, 86, 87, 89) with no corresponding pattern days 8–9 suggest a procedural or environmental change local to day 10. Operator fatigue, a minor change in launch angle, or increased air currents could bias period upward in isolated trials. This is less reproducible and harder to validate independently than temperature, and does not explain the lack of outliers in days 8–9.

hypotheses.label: Legitimate physical period increase (gravitational or environmental change)
hypotheses.rationale: Settlement or apparatus subsidence, or a change in local gravity field, would increase periods reproducibly. However, this is speculative without independent geophysical data and contradicts the expectation that Meridian's baseline apparatus is on stable ground. Days 8–9 show no trend supporting this. Reserved here only because baseline-building must remain open to site-level anomalies.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Previous review held 'no active hypotheses' because baseline data appeared stable through day 10.
